# Optimization Procedures

Also called: Compute Matching at Intervals, Interval-based Optimal Transport Update, Optimal Transport Matching Interval (K), matching interval

## Overview
This family defines the iterative optimization procedure that embeds a differentiable renderer within an optimizer to estimate scene parameters (pose, geometry, materials, illumination) from observed images or measurements [S1]. It solves the inverse problem of reconstructing 3D structure and appearance by minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground-truth observations [S5, S14, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing the fundamental control flow—sampling, [forward rendering](#1816-per-voxel-projection-object-order.md), loss computation, and gradient update—that all specific training strategies (such as [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) loops, stage-based training, or black-box baselines) instantiate. Unlike [Optimization Procedures](7150-optimization-procedures.md) which focuses on computational efficiency via transportation matrices, this family focuses on the convergence dynamics and parameter update mechanics of the inverse problem itself.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

The standard [emission-absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md) computes the color $\hat{C}(\mathbf{r})$ for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]:

$$
\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)) \mathbf{c}_i
$$

where $\sigma_i$ is the density, $\delta_i$ is the step size, $\mathbf{c}_i$ is the color, and $T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$ is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]:
1. **Reverse-Mode [Automatic Differentiation](#7151-automatic-differentiation-reverse-adjoint-mode.md) (AD):** Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing $O(kn)$ intermediate states (where $n$ is pixels and $k$ is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
2. **[Adjoint Method](#789-adjoint-method.md):** Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
3. **Analytic Inversion / Explicit Gradients:** Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to $O(n)$ by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

## Subtopics

### [Color Volume Optimization and Density Initialization](842-color-volume-optimization-and-density-initialization.md)
This method addresses the non-convex optimization problem inherent in reconstructing 3D density fields using non-monotonic transfer functions (TFs) within an emission-absorption model. Standard density initialization often leads to local minima where gradients point away from the true solution, particularly when the TF is Gaussian-like. It solves this by first optimizing a "color volume" (storing RGB emission and scalar absorption directly) to bypass TF-induced local minima, and then estimating a density volume from this color volume to serve as a high-quality initialization for the final density optimization. It sets itself apart from standard zero-initialization or random noise initialization by analytically deriving a bias term that ensures the initial activated alpha value is very close to zero, effectively initializing the scene with low density.

### [Regularization losses](1413-regularization-losses.md)
[Regularization losses](#1413-regularization-losses.md) are auxiliary objective terms added to the training of [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) to constrain the solution space, prevent overfitting to noisy input data, and enforce physical or perceptual plausibility. While the primary [data consistency loss](#2976-data-consistency-loss.md) ensures the rendered output matches the input observations, regularization losses address the ill-posed nature of inverse rendering by penalizing undesirable properties such as high-frequency noise, geometric inconsistency, or implausible density distributions. They set themselves apart from sibling methods like [Photometric Reconstruction Loss](7799-photometric-reconstruction-loss.md) by targeting the internal scene representation or the statistical properties of the rendering weights rather than the pixel-wise color error directly.

### [Optimization Loops and Training Procedures](5622-optimization-loops-and-training-procedures.md)
This family defines the iterative optimization procedure that embeds a differentiable renderer within an optimizer to estimate scene parameters (pose, geometry, materials, illumination) from observed images or measurements. It solves the inverse problem of reconstructing 3D structure and appearance by minimizing the difference between rendered images and ground-truth observations. It sets itself apart from its siblings by providing the fundamental control flow—sampling, forward rendering, loss computation, and gradient update—that all specific training strategies (such as NeRF loops, stage-based training, or black-box baselines) instantiate. Unlike [Optimization Procedures](7150-optimization-procedures.md) which focuses on computational efficiency via transportation matrices, this family focuses on the convergence dynamics and parameter update mechanics of the inverse problem itself.

### [Active Set Method for OIT-based 3DGS](7528-active-set-method-for-oit-based-3dgs.md)
The [Active Set Method for OIT-based 3DGS](#7528-active-set-method-for-oit-based-3dgs.md) (SparseOIT) is an optimization strategy that accelerates the training of Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) based 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) by exploiting the sparsity of variable dependencies among Gaussian splats. Unlike standard 3DGS which sorts all Gaussians per pixel, SparseOIT removes the depth sorting step entirely and freezes Gaussians that have converged or contribute negligibly to the gradient, optimizing only a subset of "active" variables. This approach achieves comparable novel-view quality to volumetric rendering methods while significantly outperforming existing OIT-based methods in training speed.

### [Photometric Reconstruction Loss](7799-photometric-reconstruction-loss.md)
The loss function used to minimize the difference between rendered pixels and input training images during joint optimization.

## Background
The concept of optimizing radiance fields through differentiable rendering was pioneered by Mildenhall et al. in 2020 with [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRF) [S1]. The specific optimization procedure of computing pixel matching (transportation matrix) at intervals rather than every iteration was introduced in "Differentiable Rendering Using [RGBXY Derivatives and Optimal Transport](#8830-rgbxy-derivatives-with-optimal-transport-drot.md)" [S1]. This method identified that computing pixel matching is a computational bottleneck and that matching changes subtly between adjacent iterations. By computing matching once every $K+1$ steps (with $K=5$ as a default), the method accelerates optimization by 4× to 5× without hurting accuracy [S1]. The hybrid strategy combining RGBXY derivatives and standard derivatives was also introduced in this work, using RGBXY for the first 75% of iterations and standard derivatives for the last 25% [S1].
